dek: Audible sold spoken-word audio as downloads, years before most people owned a device that could play them.
lede: Audible started with a simple idea: people who could not sit down with a book could still listen to one. In 1999 that idea ran ahead of the hardware. Most audiobooks lived on cassettes and CDs, home internet ran over dial-up modems, and the iPod was still two years away. Audible had built its own small player to carry the files, and it sold subscriptions to books, magazines, and radio programs delivered through the web.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Don Katz, a journalist and author, founded Audible in New Jersey in 1995. His bet was that spoken word belonged on the internet, not on plastic. The company signed rights to books and periodicals, recorded much of its own catalog, and shipped the Audible Mobile Player in 1997. The device was clumsy and the downloads were slow, but the model was set: a library of audio, paid for by the title or by subscription, ready whenever the listener was.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Audible priced its offering at $9 a share in July 1999. The years after were hard, and the stock fell far below its offer price when the dot-com bubble burst. A deal to supply audiobooks to Apple's iTunes Store in 2003 gave the company the device it had always needed. Amazon bought Audible in 2008 for about $300 million, and the brand became the default place to buy an audiobook.

cover.theme: a lute player (music for the ear)

dek: NIC built and ran official state government websites, paid for by small fees on online transactions.
lede: In 1999 most dealings with a state government still meant a line at an office counter. NIC offered states a different deal. It would build and run their official websites at no upfront cost, and it would earn its money from small fees on services like driving records and business filings. The company began in Kansas and by its offering it had signed several states, betting that public services would follow commerce onto the web.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Jeffery Fraser started the business in Kansas in the early 1990s as the Kansas Information Consortium. The model was self-funding: a state gave NIC a contract, NIC paid to build the portal, and fees from frequent users, often lawyers, insurers, and lenders, covered the cost. That removed the biggest obstacle for state agencies, which rarely had technology budgets to spare. Each new state contract became a long-running source of revenue.

sections.heading: The Road to the Bell
sections.body: NIC priced its offering at $12 a share in July 1999. Like many internet stocks it fell hard in 2000, but the business underneath kept growing quietly. State by state, NIC added portals and services until it ran official websites for a large share of American states. Tyler Technologies, a maker of software for local governments, bought NIC in 2021 for about $2.3 billion.

fate: Taken private by Vista Equity Partners, 2014 ($4.3B)
dek: TIBCO sold software that moved information between computer systems in real time, starting on Wall Street trading floors.
lede: TIBCO took its name from "The Information Bus", software that let separate computer systems publish and receive messages the instant something changed. The technology began on Wall Street trading floors in the late 1980s, where a delay of seconds cost money. By 1999 large companies of every kind faced the same problem across their own systems, and the arrival of the web made it more urgent. Reuters owned a majority of TIBCO when it went public.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Vivek Ranadivé built the information bus at his earlier company, Teknekron Software Systems, which Reuters bought in 1994. TIBCO Software became its own company in 1997 to sell the technology beyond finance. The bet was that every business would need what traders needed: data that arrived as events happened, not in nightly batches. TIBCO pitched the idea under the name "the event-driven enterprise" and sold it to banks, telecom companies, and manufacturers.

sections.heading: The Road to the Bell
sections.body: TIBCO priced its offering at $15 a share in July 1999, and the stock climbed sharply through the following year. It fell with the rest of the market in 2001, but the company stayed profitable and grew by acquisition, adding integration, analytics, and visualization products. In 2014 Vista Equity Partners took TIBCO private for about $4.3 billion. It later became part of Cloud Software Group alongside Citrix.

cover.theme: a fast mail coach (the information bus)

dek: Ask Jeeves let people type questions in plain English and answered through a cartoon butler.
lede: Early search engines expected people to think like librarians and type keywords. Ask Jeeves asked them to type a question, as they would to a person. A friendly cartoon butler stood on the home page, and editors behind the scenes matched common questions to good answers. When the company went public in the summer of 1999, the web was full of new users who found keyword search confusing, and Jeeves was one of the most recognized faces online.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Garrett Gruener, a venture capitalist, and David Warthen, a software engineer, started the company in Berkeley in 1996. Their bet was that plain language would win over keywords. The system combined software that parsed questions with a large library of answers that people had written and checked. The butler, borrowed from P. G. Wodehouse's fictional valet, gave the service a personality that set it apart from the plainer search pages of the day.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Ask Jeeves priced its offering at $14 a share on July 1, 1999, and the stock soared on its first day of trading. Google soon showed that good ranking mattered more than plain-language parsing, and Ask Jeeves bought the Teoma search engine in 2001 to keep up. IAC acquired the company in 2005 for about $1.85 billion. The butler retired in 2006, and the service carried on as Ask.com.

cover.theme: a valet with a coffee pot (the butler)
cover.artwork: Study of Valet with Coffee Pot

dek: E-Loan let borrowers compare and apply for mortgages online, with rates shown openly instead of hidden behind a broker.
lede: In 1999 buying a house usually meant a mortgage broker, a stack of paper, and fees that few borrowers understood. E-Loan put the process on the web. Borrowers could compare rates from many lenders, apply online, and track their loan as it moved toward closing. The company was part of a wave of firms trying to bring finance online, and it argued that open pricing would win the trust of buyers who felt brokers kept them in the dark.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Chris Larsen and Janina Pawlowski, who had worked together in mortgage brokerage, founded E-Loan in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1996. Their bet was transparency. E-Loan showed borrowers the rates it got and the fees it charged, which was unusual at the time. It earned money as a broker, and the internet let it serve borrowers anywhere at a lower cost than a branch office.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: E-Loan priced its offering at $14 a share in June 1999. The stock fell steeply when the bubble burst, but the business survived and later turned a profit as low interest rates drove a refinancing boom. Popular, Inc., the Puerto Rico banking group, acquired E-Loan in 2005. Chris Larsen went on to co-found the lending marketplace Prosper and later Ripple.

tagline: The Post Office on Your Desk
dek: Stamps.com let people buy and print official U.S. postage from their own computers and printers.
lede: For more than a century, buying postage meant a trip to the post office or a leased postage meter. In 1999 the U.S. Postal Service began testing a new idea: postage that a customer could buy over the internet and print with an ordinary printer. Stamps.com was one of the first companies approved to sell it. It went public that June, aiming at small businesses and home offices that mailed often but had little reason to own a meter.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was that a printer and an internet connection could replace the postage meter. Stamps.com handled the security the Postal Service demanded, encoding each printed stamp with a barcode that proved it was paid for. Customers paid a monthly fee for the software and service. The pitch was convenience: no lines, no meter lease, and postage ready any time of day.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Stamps.com priced its offering at $11 a share in June 1999, and the stock rose fast before falling hard in the crash that followed. The company cut costs, outlasted rivals, and found steady growth in shipping labels for online sellers. It bought ShipStation and other shipping tools as e-commerce grew. Thoma Bravo took Stamps.com private in 2021 for about $6.6 billion.

cover.theme: a woman with a letter (the mail)

dek: Juniper Networks built high-speed routers for internet carriers, the first serious challenger to Cisco in the core of the network.
lede: By 1999 internet traffic was doubling at a pace that strained the routers at its core. Those machines came almost entirely from Cisco, and many were general-purpose computers asked to do a very specialized job. Juniper offered a router built from the ground up for the backbone, with custom chips that forwarded packets at full line speed. Its first product had shipped only months before the company went public, and carriers were already lining up to test it.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Pradeep Sindhu, a computer scientist from Xerox PARC, founded Juniper in 1996. His bet was that the internet core needed purpose-built hardware, not software running on general processors. Juniper split the router into two parts: a control plane for routing decisions and a forwarding engine in silicon that moved packets. Its M40 router, released in 1998, handled far more traffic per box than competitors and won early customers among large carriers.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Juniper priced its offering at $34 a share in June 1999, and it became one of the most successful offerings of the era. The stock soared through 2000 as carriers raced to build capacity, then fell sharply when the telecom bubble burst. Juniper survived as Cisco's main rival in carrier and data center networking for a quarter century. Hewlett Packard Enterprise completed its purchase of Juniper in 2025 for about $14 billion.

cover.theme: a cypress, kin of the juniper

tagline: The Cash Register of the Web
dek: CyberSource processed credit card payments and screened for fraud on behalf of online merchants.
lede: In 1999 a business that wanted to sell online had to solve a hard problem on its own: how to accept a credit card from a stranger and know it was real. CyberSource offered that as a service. A merchant's website passed the order to CyberSource, which authorized the card, checked for fraud, and handled tax and export rules. It was one of the first companies to sell payment processing over the internet to other internet companies.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: William McKiernan started CyberSource in 1996 inside software.net, an early online software store. The store had built tools to take payments and spot fraud, and McKiernan saw that other merchants needed the same tools. The bet was that the plumbing of online commerce would be a business of its own. CyberSource charged per transaction, so it grew as online shopping grew.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: CyberSource priced its offering at $11 a share in June 1999. The stock climbed fast and then collapsed with the dot-com crash, but the company kept its core business and stayed independent. It bought Authorize.Net in 2007, adding thousands of small merchants. Visa acquired CyberSource in 2010 for about $2 billion, and the name lives on as Visa's platform for online payments.

cover.artwork: The Merchant (Sho) from the series Beauties Illustrating the Four Classes

dek: Ariba sold software that let large companies buy supplies online and later ran a network linking buyers and suppliers.
lede: Large companies spend huge sums on everyday supplies, from pens to computers, and in the 1990s most of it ran through paper forms and phone calls. Ariba put that buying on the web. Employees chose items from an online catalog, managers approved them, and orders went to suppliers electronically. When Ariba went public in June 1999, business-to-business commerce was the hottest idea on Wall Street, and Ariba was its clearest example.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Keith Krach and a group of co-founders started Ariba in 1996 in Silicon Valley. The bet was that procurement, a dull back-office task, was a large market waiting for the web. Ariba's software cut the cost of processing a purchase order and helped companies steer spending to preferred suppliers. Ariba also built a network so that suppliers could connect once and reach many buyers.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Ariba priced its offering at $23 a share in June 1999, and the stock soared on its first day of trading. At its peak the company was worth tens of billions of dollars, and then it lost most of that value when the bubble burst. Ariba cut costs and refocused on its supplier network, which became its lasting strength. SAP bought Ariba in 2012 for about $4.3 billion.

cover.theme: a harbor (where buyers and sellers meet)
cover.artwork: Ships in the Harbor at Sète

tagline: Trades at the Speed of a Click
dek: onlinetradinginc.com was a small Florida discount brokerage that let customers buy and sell stocks over the internet.
lede: In 1999 online trading was one of the defining stories of the bull market. Millions of people opened accounts with internet brokers, and low commissions drew a new crowd of active traders. onlinetradinginc.com was a small player in this boom, a Florida brokerage that sold self-directed trading through its website. It went public in June 1999 with a modest offering, hoping to grow as more investors moved their accounts online.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was simple: as trading moved to the web, a lean online broker could win customers on price and service. Like its competitors, the firm earned money from commissions on each trade, so its revenue rose and fell with the market's mood. Smaller brokers like this one faced well-funded rivals that spent heavily on advertising to win accounts. Price and speed were its main selling points.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: onlinetradinginc.com priced its offering at $7 a share in June 1999, one of the smaller deals of that busy summer. Trading volume fell when the market turned in 2000, which put pressure on every online broker that lived on commissions. The industry consolidated quickly in the years that followed, as larger firms bought up smaller ones and fought over price. Its story is a reminder of how crowded that corner of the boom became.

cover.theme: speculators trading at the Palais Royal
cover.artwork: Study for The Speculators at the Palais Royal

dek: BackWeb built push software that delivered updates and content to computers in the background, without users asking for it.
lede: In the late 1990s, "push" was one of the most hyped ideas on the internet. Instead of making people visit websites, push software would send news, updates, and files straight to their computers. BackWeb, an Israeli company, built one of the leading push systems. By the time it went public in 1999 the consumer hype had faded, and BackWeb sold its technology to companies that needed to send information and software to their own employees.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Eli Barkat co-founded BackWeb in 1995 with backing from BRM, the Israeli technology group he ran with his brother Nir. The bet was that the web should come to the user. BackWeb's software used spare network capacity to deliver content quietly, so it did not slow people down. Large companies used it to send sales materials, software patches, and alerts across their networks.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: BackWeb priced its offering at $12 a share in June 1999. The stock rose with the market and then fell when the bubble burst and companies cut spending. BackWeb moved toward software that let laptop users work offline with web applications. Eli Barkat left the chief executive role in 2003 and returned to venture capital. BackWeb remained a small company in the years that followed.

cover.theme: a spider's web (the web that comes to you)
cover.artwork: Woman with Spider's Web Between Bare Trees

tagline: Calm at the Eye of the Storm
dek: F5 Networks made load balancers that spread web traffic across many servers so busy websites stayed up.
lede: In 1999 the busiest websites were learning that one server was never enough. Traffic arrived in surges, and a single overloaded machine could take a whole site down. F5 Networks sold a box that sat in front of a group of servers and sent each visitor to the one best able to respond. The company named itself after the strongest class of tornado, and it went public as websites raced to handle the flood of new users.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Michael Almquist and Jeff Hussey founded F5 in Seattle in 1996. The bet was that websites would become critical services that could not fail. Their product, BIG-IP, checked the health of each server and routed traffic around failures. It turned a rack of ordinary machines into one reliable website. Online retailers, portals, and banks were among the early customers. Its customers needed their sites up at every hour of the day.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: F5 priced its offering at $10 a share in June 1999. The stock climbed through the boom and then fell sharply in 2000 and 2001, when many of its dot-com customers disappeared. F5 rebuilt around large enterprises and service providers and added security and application delivery features. It became one of the long-term survivors of its class and remains a public company today.

dek: Network Access Solutions sold DSL broadband to businesses across the Mid-Atlantic, over existing telephone lines.
lede: In 1999 a new law and a new technology opened the local phone network to competition. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 let upstart carriers rent lines from the regional phone companies, and DSL let those old copper lines carry fast internet. Network Access Solutions was one of these competitive carriers. Based in Virginia, it focused on businesses in the Bell Atlantic region and went public in June 1999 to fund a rapid build-out.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was that small and medium businesses would pay for always-on internet that was far faster than dial-up and cheaper than a leased line. Network Access Solutions placed its equipment in phone company central offices and sold service directly and through internet providers. Growth required heavy spending before customers arrived, which made the business dependent on open capital markets.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Network Access Solutions priced its offering at $12 a share in June 1999. When the telecom bubble burst in 2000, the money that funded carriers like it dried up. The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in June 2002. DSL.net bought its network assets and business customers in early 2003. Its network lived on, but the company that built it did not. It joined a long list of DSL carriers that failed when the money ran out.

cover.theme: a copper mine canyon (old copper lines)
cover.artwork: Bingham Canon, Telegraph Mine, near Salt Lake Utah

fate: Sold its operations to Charter Communications, 2002
dek: High Speed Access Corp. ran cable-modem internet service for cable operators in smaller towns and rural markets.
lede: In 1999 cable-modem internet was the fastest way to get online at home, but it reached mostly big cities. Large cable companies had partners and capital to offer it. Smaller cable systems in small towns often did not. High Speed Access Corp. filled that gap. It upgraded those systems, ran the service, handled customer support, and split the revenue with the cable operator. It went public in June 1999 with strong backing from Paul Allen's Vulcan Ventures.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was that broadband would spread beyond the big cities, and that someone would need to bring it there. High Speed Access offered small cable operators a turnkey service, so they did not need their own technical teams. Its largest partner was Charter Communications, another company in Paul Allen's orbit, which made the relationship both a strength and a risk.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: High Speed Access priced its offering at $13 a share in June 1999. The model needed heavy spending in each new town, and losses mounted when capital grew scarce in 2000. In 2001 the company agreed to sell its operations to Charter, which completed the purchase in February 2002 for about $73 million in cash and assumed liabilities. The deal left the company with little more than cash and the task of winding down its affairs.

dek: EDGAR Online repackaged public SEC filings into searchable, alert-driven data products for investors and professionals.
lede: When the Securities and Exchange Commission put its EDGAR database online in the mid-1990s, every public company filing became free to read. Free did not mean easy. The raw documents were long, plain text, and hard to search. EDGAR Online turned them into a service, with alerts, search tools, and data extracted from financial statements. In 1999 a new wave of individual investors was reading filings for the first time, and EDGAR Online aimed to be their guide.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Susan and Marc Strausberg founded the company in Connecticut in 1995. The bet was that public data was valuable once someone organized it. EDGAR Online sold subscriptions to investors, lawyers, and analysts, and licensed its data to websites and financial firms. It added value by tagging, indexing, and delivering the filings faster and in friendlier formats than the government site.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: EDGAR Online priced its offering at $9.50 a share in May 1999. The company never grew large, and it spent years building tools for XBRL, the tagged data format the SEC later required for financial statements. RR Donnelley, the financial printing company, acquired EDGAR Online in 2012. By then the idea of machine-readable financial data, which EDGAR Online had promoted for years, had become a regulatory requirement. Its products and data joined the larger company's financial services business, and the EDGAR Online brand continued for a time.

cover.artwork: The Raven on the Bust of Pallas

dek: Redback Networks made the systems that let phone and cable carriers sign up and manage millions of broadband subscribers.
lede: In 1999 phone companies were rolling out DSL and needed a way to manage a flood of new customers. Each subscriber had to be logged in, given an address, and routed to the right internet provider. Redback Networks built the box that did this, called the Subscriber Management System. It sat at the edge of the carrier network, and it went public in May 1999 as broadband was moving from trial to mass market.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Redback was founded in 1996 in Silicon Valley. The bet was that broadband would create a new layer of the network, between the access lines and the internet core, and that this layer needed its own equipment. Redback's SMS product won quick adoption among carriers deploying DSL. It was one of the most celebrated networking start-ups of its moment. Its name came from the redback spider, a fitting emblem for a company spinning connections across the web.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Redback priced its offering at $23 a share in May 1999, and the stock leapt on its first day. It bought Siara Systems in 1999 in a stock deal worth billions, and its value soared before the telecom crash erased most of it. Redback restructured through a prepackaged bankruptcy in 2003 and emerged as a smaller company. Ericsson acquired Redback in 2007 for about $2.1 billion.

tagline: The Mall in a Teenager's Pocket
dek: Alloy combined a teen clothing catalog with a website and community aimed at teenage girls.
lede: In 1999 teenagers were the first generation to grow up online, and marketers were eager to reach them. Alloy built a business around girls aged roughly 10 to 24. It mailed a fashion catalog to millions of homes and ran a website with quizzes, chat, and content written in their voice. The catalog paid the bills, and the website built loyalty. Alloy went public in May 1999 as the company that understood teens on the web.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Matt Diamond and James Johnson founded Alloy in New York in 1996. The bet was that a brand could be both a store and a gathering place for young people. Alloy used its website to grow its customer list and its catalog to turn that audience into sales. Advertisers that wanted to reach teens also paid for access to the community.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Alloy priced its offering at $15 a share in May 1999. As the dot-com market cooled, it moved toward marketing and media services, and it bought magazines, school marketing programs, and a book packager. That unit, Alloy Entertainment, developed series such as Gossip Girl and Pretty Little Liars. ZelnickMedia took Alloy private in 2010. The company had come a long way from a catalog and a chat room, and it showed how a youth brand could become a media business.

dek: Copper Mountain Networks built DSL equipment that let new carriers sell fast internet over ordinary phone lines.
lede: By 1999 a new kind of phone company was racing to sell DSL. These competitive carriers rented copper phone lines from the old monopolies and installed their own equipment in central offices. Copper Mountain Networks made that equipment, the access concentrators that turned plain copper into broadband. Its customers were the fastest-growing carriers of the moment, and it went public in May 1999 with sales rising quickly.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Copper Mountain was founded in 1996. The bet was that the copper already running into every home and office could carry far more than voice. Its systems packed many DSL lines into a small space, which mattered in crowded central offices where carriers paid by the square foot. Covad and NorthPoint, two of the largest new DSL carriers, were major buyers.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Copper Mountain priced its offering at $21 a share in May 1999, and the stock rose sharply through the following year. Then its customers began to fail. When the competitive carriers went bankrupt or slowed in 2000 and 2001, Copper Mountain's sales collapsed. Tut Systems acquired the company in 2005 in a stock deal valued at about $10 million. Its fate tracked its customers' fate almost exactly.

dek: Portal Software made billing systems that let internet and telecom providers charge customers for online services.
lede: In 1999 internet providers faced a basic problem. Old telephone billing systems were built to charge for minutes of voice calls, not for web access, email accounts, or content. Portal Software sold a billing platform designed for the internet. It could track usage, apply complex pricing plans, and produce bills for millions of customers. As every carrier rushed to sell online services, Portal went public in May 1999 promising to be the cash register behind them.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: John Little started the company in 1985 as a consulting firm, and it built billing tools for early online services. The bet was that internet services would need flexible, real-time billing, and that carriers would buy it rather than build it. Portal's Infranet product ran on standard servers and could change pricing quickly, which carriers launching new services valued. That speed mattered in a market where new products appeared every month.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Portal priced its offering at $14 a share in May 1999, and its stock rose sharply in the boom. When carriers cut spending in 2001, Portal's sales fell and its losses grew. Accounting problems later forced restatements and a delisting from the Nasdaq. Oracle acquired Portal in 2006, and its billing software became part of Oracle's communications products. The billing problem Portal set out to solve never went away.

cover.artwork: Coventry, St. Mary's Hall, Entrance Gateway

dek: Silknet sold software that helped large companies serve customers across the web, email, and phone.
lede: By 1999 customers expected companies to answer them by email and on the web, not just by phone. Most companies had no good system to track those conversations. Silknet, a New Hampshire software company, sold a platform it called eService. It gave support agents and customers a shared view of questions, answers, and history across channels. Silknet went public in May 1999 as businesses scrambled to serve customers online.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was that customer service would become a web business, and that companies would need software to run it. Silknet's platform let customers find answers on their own and passed harder questions to human agents with the full history attached. It sold to large companies that handled huge volumes of support requests. The name suggested a fine, strong thread connecting a company to each of its customers. Large firms in telecom, technology, and finance were among the buyers.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Silknet priced its offering at $15 a share in May 1999, and the stock climbed quickly in the boom. In 2000 Kana Communications agreed to buy Silknet in an all-stock deal valued at billions of dollars at signing. The value of that deal fell sharply as internet stocks collapsed later that year. The merger made Silknet's eService suite part of Kana's product line. Kana itself struggled through the downturn that followed, and the combined company spent years trying to recover the momentum of 1999.

cover.artwork: Spinning Cloth, Preparing Tea Leaves, Preparing Silk

dek: WorldGate Communications delivered internet access and email through cable television set-top boxes.
lede: In 1999 most American homes had a television and a cable box, but far fewer had a personal computer. WorldGate wanted to bring the internet to the TV instead. Its service ran through existing cable set-top boxes, so viewers could check email or browse the web with a remote and a wireless keyboard. It also let a TV show or ad link straight to a related website. WorldGate went public in April 1999 with cable operators as partners.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was that the television, not the PC, would be most people's door to the internet. WorldGate's system did the heavy work on servers at the cable company, so it could run on boxes already in living rooms. Cable operators saw it as a way to sell a new service without new hardware in every home. It was an early attempt at the connected television that many companies would try again in later decades.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: WorldGate priced its offering at $21 a share in April 1999. Interactive TV proved a hard sell, and cheap PCs and broadband pulled people toward computers instead. WorldGate shifted its focus to video phones in the 2000s. It remained small and struggled financially in the years after its offering. Its offering came at the high point of enthusiasm for interactive TV. The idea of watching and browsing on the same screen would return years later, carried by smart TVs and streaming boxes rather than by cable set-top boxes.

dek: Extreme Networks built fast Ethernet switches that pushed gigabit speeds into corporate networks.
lede: In 1999 corporate networks were straining under new traffic from the web, email, and file sharing. Ethernet, the standard for local networks, had just reached gigabit speeds. Extreme Networks built switches that delivered that speed at a lower cost per port than older designs. Its Summit and BlackDiamond lines used custom chips to switch traffic at full speed. Extreme went public in April 1999, the second wave of a networking boom.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Gordon Stitt, Stephen Haddock, and Herb Schneider founded Extreme in 1996. The bet was that Ethernet would scale from the desktop to the network core, and that a focused start-up could beat bigger rivals on speed and price. Extreme built its switches around custom chips that handled routing and switching in hardware. Customers ranged from universities to data centers. The company competed head on with Cisco and with other new switch makers.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Extreme priced its offering at $17 a share in April 1999, and the stock rose sharply through 2000 before falling with the market. The company survived the crash and grew by acquisition in later years, buying wireless and data center businesses from Motorola, Avaya, and Brocade. Extreme remains a public company today. It moved its headquarters from Silicon Valley to North Carolina.

dek: Claimsnet.com processed medical insurance claims over the internet for doctors and other healthcare providers.
lede: American healthcare has always run on paper, and in the 1990s insurance claims were among the heaviest piles. Each doctor's visit produced a form that had to be checked, coded, and sent to the right insurer. Claimsnet.com offered small medical practices a way to do this over the web. Providers entered claims in a browser, and Claimsnet checked them and sent them on electronically. It went public in April 1999 as healthcare moved online.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was that small medical offices would use the web to cut the cost and delay of filing claims. Large hospitals already had expensive systems for this work, but smaller practices often still used paper. Claimsnet charged by the claim and promised faster payment with fewer errors. Its pitch was simple: a browser and an internet connection were all a practice needed.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Claimsnet.com priced its offering at $8 a share in April 1999. The company stayed small, and the healthcare internet market proved slower and more crowded than investors had hoped. Its stock later moved off the Nasdaq to the over-the-counter market. Claimsnet continued to operate in claims processing as a small company. It never reached the scale its offering had promised, but it showed how early the industry tried to move claims onto the web.

fate: Taken private by its largest shareholders, 2008
dek: Critical Path ran email systems for internet providers, telecom carriers, and large companies as an outsourced service.
lede: In 1999 email was becoming the most important application on the internet, and running it well was hard. Internet providers, phone companies, and large businesses all needed mail servers that could handle millions of accounts without failing. Critical Path offered to run email for them. Customers kept their own brand, and Critical Path handled the servers, storage, and spam. It went public in March 1999 as one of the first companies to sell email as a hosted service.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: David Hayden founded Critical Path in San Francisco in 1997. The bet was that email was too important and too complex for most companies to run themselves. Critical Path built large data centers for mail and signed deals with carriers and portals. Its business was an early version of what later became cloud computing. Customers paid by the mailbox, so revenue grew with every new account.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Critical Path priced its offering at $24 a share in March 1999, and the stock soared through 2000. Then an accounting scandal in 2001 forced restatements, and several former employees were later convicted. The company survived and shifted to selling messaging software to carriers. Its major shareholders took it private in 2008, and it later merged with Mirapoint. Openwave Messaging bought the combined company in 2013.

cover.theme: a mail stagecoach on the road

dek: iVillage was an online network of communities and content aimed at women, covering health, parenting, money, and work.
lede: In the late 1990s the web was still seen as a place built by and for young men. iVillage set out to change that. Its sites and message boards covered parenting, health, careers, and relationships, and women used them to trade advice with each other. When it went public in March 1999, iVillage was among the largest destinations for women online and one of the most watched media start-ups in New York.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Candice Carpenter, Nancy Evans, and Robert Levitan founded iVillage in New York in 1995. The bet was that women would come online for community, not just content. The founders built the site around message boards where members helped each other, then sold advertising and sponsorships to brands that wanted to reach those women. Early investors included America Online. That focus set iVillage apart from portals built for a general audience.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: iVillage priced its offering at $24 a share in March 1999, and the stock more than doubled on its first day. Losses were heavy in the years that followed, and the share price fell sharply when the bubble burst. iVillage cut costs, bought rival Women.com, and eventually turned a profit. NBC Universal acquired the company in 2006 for about $600 million. Its message boards had long outlasted the hype that surrounded its debut.

dek: Intraware sold and delivered business software electronically, then sold its delivery platform to other software makers.
lede: In 1999 business software still arrived in boxes, on CDs, with license keys printed on paper. Intraware, based in the San Francisco Bay Area, wanted to move that process online. It resold software from major vendors and delivered it over the internet, with the licenses tracked in one place. When Intraware went public in February 1999, it was betting that software would become something companies downloaded, not something they unpacked.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was that software delivery and licensing were messy enough to be a business of their own. Intraware built a service called SubscribeNet that let software makers deliver products and updates to customers, and track who was entitled to what. Over time this platform became more important than its reselling business. Its customers included large companies that bought software from many vendors.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Intraware priced its offering at $16 a share in February 1999. The stock rose in the boom and then fell hard. The company dropped reselling and focused on SubscribeNet, selling it to software makers as a service. Acresso Software, later renamed Flexera, acquired Intraware in January 2009 for $4.00 a share in cash. SubscribeNet lived on inside Flexera's licensing products, which still serve many software makers.

dek: Vignette sold content management software that let large websites publish and personalize pages at scale.
lede: In 1999 big websites were growing faster than anyone could update them by hand. Newspapers, retailers, and banks needed a way for editors to publish thousands of pages and change them daily. Vignette sold software that did this. Its StoryServer product stored content in a database and built web pages on demand, and it could tailor pages to each visitor. Vignette went public in February 1999 as one of the stars of Austin's growing tech scene.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Ross Garber founded Vignette in Austin in 1995. The bet was that websites would become as complex as publishing houses and would need software to match. Vignette sold to media companies first, then to any business with a large website. It charged high license fees, and the market for its product grew as every major company moved online. Its product was expensive and complex, but for a large website in 1999 there were few alternatives.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Vignette priced its offering at $19 a share in February 1999, and the stock soared through the following year. At its peak the company was worth billions of dollars. Then the market crashed, and cheaper content tools crowded in. Vignette shrank but stayed in business for a decade. Open Text acquired it in 2009 for about $310 million. Its story traced the full arc of the enterprise software boom.

cover.artwork: Vignettes of Labor (Weaving, Fishing, Digging, Painting)

fate: Merged with WebMD, 1999; continued as WebMD
dek: Healtheon aimed to connect doctors, insurers, and patients online to cut the paperwork and cost of American healthcare.
lede: By 1999 Jim Clark had already co-founded Silicon Graphics and Netscape. His third company, Healtheon, took aim at the most paper-bound industry in America. Healthcare spent huge sums on claims, referrals, and approvals that moved by fax and phone. Healtheon wanted to connect every doctor, insurer, lab, and patient over the internet so these steps happened automatically. Its offering in February 1999 drew attention largely because of Clark's track record.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Jim Clark founded Healtheon in 1995. The bet was that the internet could take a large share of the waste out of healthcare administration. The company built software to check eligibility, submit claims, and handle referrals online. Progress was slower than planned, because healthcare had many players and few shared standards. Doctors, insurers, and hospitals each used different systems, and few saw a reason to change quickly. The vision was large, and the work to reach it was slow.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Healtheon priced its offering at $8 a share in February 1999, and the stock rose sharply that spring. Later in 1999 it merged with WebMD and several other companies, and the combined business took the WebMD name. WebMD became the best-known consumer health site in America and remained a public company until it was taken private in 2017. The original goal of cutting paperwork remained a large part of the business.

dek: VerticalNet ran dozens of online trade communities for specific industries, from chemicals to food service.
lede: In 1999 investors believed that the biggest internet opportunity lay in trade between businesses, not in selling to consumers. VerticalNet was an early leader. It ran dozens of industry websites, each a community for professionals in one field, with news, product listings, and job boards. It earned money from advertising and from deals made between suppliers and buyers. VerticalNet went public in February 1999 as the leading example of business-to-business commerce.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Michael McNulty and Douglas Alexander founded VerticalNet in Pennsylvania in 1995. The bet was that each industry would gather online in its own vertical community. VerticalNet built or bought sites for fields such as water treatment, semiconductors, and food service. The plan was to start with content and grow into trading marketplaces once buyers and sellers were in one place. Each community gave suppliers a focused audience and gave buyers a place to compare options.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: VerticalNet priced its offering at $16 a share in February 1999, and its stock rose many times over within a year. At its peak the company was worth billions of dollars. When the business-to-business bubble burst in 2000, it sold most of its communities and turned to procurement software. BravoSolution acquired VerticalNet in 2008. Its rise and fall tracked the whole business-to-business boom almost exactly.

cover.artwork: Prairie School Skyscraper, Chicago, Illinois, Perspective

dek: Tut Systems made equipment that turned existing phone wiring in buildings and homes into fast data networks.
lede: In 1999 a great deal of copper wire ran through apartment buildings, hotels, and campuses, installed for telephones. Tut Systems built products that let that wiring carry fast data as well. A hotel could offer guests internet access, or an apartment building could offer broadband, without pulling new cable. Tut also worked on home networking over phone lines. It went public in January 1999, as everyone looked for ways to reach the last few hundred feet.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was that the wires already in place were worth more than people thought. Rewiring a building was costly and slow, while Tut's equipment worked with what was already there. It sold to building owners, service providers, and phone companies that wanted to offer broadband in multi-tenant buildings. That approach saved time and money, and it suited the rush to wire buildings for the internet. Tut's products fit the needs of property owners who wanted to add a service without tearing open walls.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Tut priced its offering at $18 a share in January 1999, and the stock rose through the boom before collapsing in 2000 and 2001. The company shifted to video processing systems for telecom carriers offering television over broadband. It bought Copper Mountain Networks in 2005. Motorola acquired Tut Systems in 2007. By then Tut had become a supplier of video gear for telecom carriers, far from its roots in building wiring.

cover.artwork: Ostracon with a Drawing of a King

dek: Covad sold DSL broadband nationwide by renting phone lines from the regional Bell companies.
lede: The Telecommunications Act of 1996 forced the old Bell phone companies to rent their lines to competitors. Covad was one of the boldest companies to take up that offer. It installed DSL equipment in central offices across the country and sold fast internet over ordinary phone lines, mostly through internet providers. When Covad went public in January 1999, it was building one of the largest DSL networks in the United States.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Charles McMinn, a Silicon Valley executive, co-founded Covad in 1996. The name came from "copper value added." The bet was that the regulated phone network could become a platform for new broadband carriers. Covad raced to be first into the most markets, spending heavily on equipment and staff before most customers had signed up. It hoped to win the market before the Bell companies could respond.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Covad priced its offering at $18 a share in January 1999, and its stock rose steeply through the year. The pace was hard to sustain. Disputes with the Bell companies, unpaid bills from failing internet providers, and the telecom crash pushed Covad into Chapter 11 in 2001. It emerged and kept operating, and Platinum Equity acquired it in 2008. Its network continued to serve business customers for years after.

cover.theme: a road lined with telegraph poles (copper lines)
cover.artwork: Tree-Lined Road with Houses and Telegraph Poles in Distance

dek: Artificial Life built software robots, or bots, that could chat with website visitors and carry out simple tasks.
lede: Long before chatbots became common, Artificial Life tried to sell them. In 1998 the company offered software "robots" that could answer questions on a website, guide shoppers, or search for information on a user's behalf. The ideas drew on research in artificial intelligence and agents. The company was small, based in Boston, and its founder had roots in German AI research. It went public in December 1998 as interest in the web was surging.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Eberhard Schoneburg founded the company. The bet was that websites would need intelligent assistants to help visitors, and that companies would license software agents to provide them. Artificial Life built bots for customer service, shopping, and information retrieval. The technology was early, and the products were limited by what software of the time could understand. The company's products were early steps toward the chatbots and virtual assistants that later became common.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Artificial Life priced its offering at $8.50 a share in December 1998. The company never grew large, and the dot-com crash hit it hard. It later moved its base to Hong Kong and turned to mobile games and applications. Its shares traded on the over-the-counter market in its later years. Its early bots now read as a preview of the conversational software that arrived decades later.

cover.artwork: Large wind-up automaton of Asahina Saburo

dek: Concur made software for employee expense reports and later business travel booking, used by companies around the world.
lede: Every business trip ends with a pile of receipts and an expense report. In the 1990s that report was usually a paper form or a spreadsheet, checked by hand in a finance office. Concur sold software that moved the process online, so employees could file expenses and managers could approve them quickly. When it went public in December 1998, Concur was a small company in the Seattle area betting on a dull but universal chore.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Steve Singh, Rajeev Singh, and Mike Hilton founded the company in 1993. The bet was that expense reporting was a costly, error-prone task that every company shared. Concur first sold software that customers installed themselves, then moved to delivering it over the internet. That shift made it one of the early successes of software as a service. Large companies with many traveling employees were the natural first customers.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Concur priced its offering at $12.50 a share in December 1998. The stock fell hard after 2000, and the company nearly ran out of room. It survived by moving to a subscription service and later added travel booking through its purchase of Outtask. Concur grew into the standard tool for business travel and expenses. SAP acquired it in 2014 for about $8.3 billion. It was a long road from a small offering to one of the largest software deals of its year.

dek: InfoSpace supplied directories, search, and content to websites and later to mobile phones, under other companies' brands.
lede: In 1998 many websites wanted yellow pages, white pages, maps, and news, but few wanted to build them. InfoSpace supplied those services to other sites, which ran them under their own names. It was part of the plumbing behind many portals. When it went public in December 1998, InfoSpace was a young Seattle-area company growing fast on deals with major websites and carriers.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Naveen Jain, a former Microsoft manager, founded InfoSpace in 1996. The bet was to stay behind the scenes, licensing content and services to sites that already had users. InfoSpace earned money from advertising and fees as those sites grew. It later supplied similar services to wireless carriers as phones began to reach the internet. This model kept costs low and let the company grow quickly through partnerships.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: InfoSpace priced its offering at $15 a share in December 1998, and the stock rose dramatically. By early 2000 it was among the most valuable internet companies, and then it lost most of that value. It bought Go2Net in 2000. Lawsuits and losses followed. InfoSpace later focused on search through its Dogpile brand and renamed itself Blucora in 2012. The new name reflected a move into tax and wealth services.

cover.theme: the constellation Leo from a book of stars (a directory)
cover.artwork: The Constellation Leo, folio probably from the Kitab suwar al-kawakib al-thabita (Book of the Images of the Fixed Stars)

dek: theglobe.com was an early online community where users built personal pages, chatted, and gathered around shared interests.
lede: theglobe.com began as a project of two Cornell University students who believed the web was a place to meet people, not just to read. It offered free personal home pages, chat rooms, and forums, years before social networks became a business. By late 1998 it had millions of members and a New York headquarters. Its offering in November 1998 became one of the defining moments of the dot-com era.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Stephan Paternot and Todd Krizelman started the company while they were students at Cornell. The bet was that online communities would draw huge audiences, and that advertisers would pay to reach them. theglobe.com grew by giving users tools to publish and connect, and by buying other community and gaming sites. Its members were young, and many were building their first web page. That made the site a gathering place for a generation learning to be social online.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: theglobe.com priced its offering at $9 a share on November 13, 1998. On its first day the stock rose more than 600 percent, a record at the time. It became a symbol of the era's excess. Advertising revenue did not keep up with costs, and the stock collapsed in 2000 and 2001. The company sold or closed most of its businesses in the years that followed. Its founders went on to other ventures.

dek: eBay ran an online auction marketplace where anyone could sell nearly anything to buyers across the country.
lede: In 1998 eBay was already a strange and wonderful place. Collectors traded toys, coins, and comics, and ordinary people sold things from their attics to strangers who paid by mailed check. eBay owned no inventory and shipped nothing. It simply ran the auctions and charged a fee for each listing and sale. That made it one of the few internet companies of its day that turned a profit, and it went public in September 1998.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Pierre Omidyar, a software engineer, launched the site as AuctionWeb in 1995 from his apartment in the San Francisco Bay Area. The bet was that people would trust each other to trade if they had a fair market and a way to rate one another. eBay's feedback system let buyers and sellers build reputations. Its users grew by word of mouth. Collectors made up the earliest community, and their enthusiasm drew in everyone else.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: eBay priced its offering at $18 a share in September 1998, and the stock nearly tripled on its first day. Under Meg Whitman, eBay grew into a global marketplace, bought PayPal in 2002, and became a pillar of online commerce. It spun off PayPal in 2015. eBay remains a public company today. It grew far beyond collectibles into a global marketplace for new and used goods.

fate: Acquired by WPP as 24/7 Real Media, 2007 ($649M)
dek: 24/7 Media sold advertising across a network of websites, giving advertisers one place to buy space on many sites.
lede: In 1998 thousands of websites had audiences but no sales staff to sell ads. Advertisers, for their part, did not want to call each site one by one. 24/7 Media solved both problems. It gathered many sites into a network, sold ad space across all of them, and served the ads through its own technology. It went public in August 1998 in New York, as online advertising grew into a real industry.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was that the web's long tail of sites could be packaged and sold like a television network. 24/7 Media signed up publishers, split ad revenue with them, and used targeting tools to place ads where they would perform. It competed with DoubleClick and other networks for both advertisers and publishers. Each new site added to the network made it more useful to advertisers.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: 24/7 Media priced its offering at $14 a share in August 1998. The stock rose through the boom and then fell sharply when online ad spending collapsed in 2000 and 2001. The company merged with Real Media in 2001 and became 24/7 Real Media. WPP acquired it in 2007 for about $649 million. The deal put the network inside one of the world's largest advertising groups.

cover.theme: the moon at night (around the clock)

dek: Digital River ran online stores and software downloads for publishers and other brands, handling payment and fulfillment.
lede: In 1998 software was still sold mostly in boxes on store shelves. Digital River, based in Minneapolis, believed it would soon arrive over the internet instead. The company built and ran online stores for software publishers, handled payments, and delivered the software as a download. It also ran a network of resellers that could sell those products on their own sites. Digital River went public in August 1998.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Joel Ronning founded Digital River in 1994. The bet was that software makers would rather hand off e-commerce than build it, and that downloads would replace physical boxes. Digital River took a cut of each sale and handled the hard parts: payment, fraud, taxes, and delivery. It later served game makers, electronics brands, and other companies selling directly online. Its model gave publishers a ready-made store without building one themselves.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Digital River priced its offering at $8.50 a share in August 1998, and the stock rose sharply in the boom. It survived the crash because its revenue came from transactions. Over time it became the online store behind many large software brands. Siris Capital took Digital River private in 2015 for about $840 million. It continues to process online sales for brands around the world.

dek: Broadcast.com streamed live radio, sports, and events over the internet, years before most homes had broadband.
lede: In 1998 most people reached the internet by dial-up modem, and streaming audio was crackly and unreliable. Broadcast.com streamed it anyway. It carried hundreds of radio stations, college and professional sports, press conferences, and live events, letting people listen to hometown games from anywhere. The Dallas company went public in July 1998 and became one of the defining stocks of the early internet boom.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The company began as AudioNet, started by Chris Jaeb in 1995. Todd Wagner and Mark Cuban joined soon after and turned it into Broadcast.com. The bet was that the internet would become a broadcast medium, and that whoever controlled the content and the servers would win. Broadcast.com earned money from advertising and from companies that paid to stream their own events.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Broadcast.com priced its offering at $18 a share in July 1998, and the stock rose about 250 percent on its first day. Less than a year later, Yahoo agreed to buy the company in a stock deal worth about $5.7 billion. The deal made Mark Cuban a billionaire. Yahoo struggled to make the business work, and it faded within a few years.

dek: Broadcom designed chips for broadband communication, starting with cable modems and set-top boxes.
lede: In 1998 the race to bring broadband into homes depended on chips that could send data over cable TV lines and phone wires. Broadcom designed many of those chips. Its products sat inside cable modems, digital set-top boxes, and networking gear, turning messy analog signals into clean digital data. Broadcom did not run its own factories, it designed chips and paid others to make them. It went public in April 1998.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Henry Samueli, a UCLA professor, and Henry Nicholas, his former student, founded Broadcom in 1991. The bet was that broadband would need complete systems on a chip, combining many functions in one piece of silicon. That approach cut costs for equipment makers and made Broadcom a key supplier for cable modems and Ethernet. Broadcom also built a reputation for hiring top engineers and for aggressive competition.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Broadcom priced its offering at $24 a share in April 1998, and the stock soared with the broadband boom. It grew into one of the largest chip companies in the world, adding Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and networking chips. In 2016 Avago Technologies acquired Broadcom for about $37 billion. The combined company took the Broadcom name. The deal was one of the largest in the history of the chip industry.

dek: Internet Security Systems sold software that scanned networks for weaknesses and detected intruders in real time.
lede: In 1998 companies were connecting their networks to the internet faster than they could secure them. Firewalls kept some threats out, but few tools could find weak spots inside or spot an attack in progress. Internet Security Systems, based in Atlanta, sold both. Its scanners checked networks for known holes, and its RealSecure product watched traffic for signs of attack. The company went public in March 1998 as ISS Group.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Christopher Klaus wrote the first version of Internet Scanner while he was a student at Georgia Tech, and he founded ISS in 1994. The bet was that security would become a constant process, not a one-time setup. ISS built a research team that tracked new vulnerabilities and updated its products to find them. Its customers included banks, government agencies, and large corporations. That research team, later called X-Force, became one of the best-known names in security.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: ISS priced its offering at $22 a share in March 1998, and its stock rose through the internet boom. The company grew into one of the largest pure security vendors, adding managed security services. IBM acquired ISS in 2006 for about $1.3 billion, and its technology became part of IBM's security business. Its founder had built a security leader from a student project.

tagline: Twice the Ad, Half the Guess
dek: DoubleClick served and targeted banner ads across thousands of websites, becoming the backbone of early online advertising.
lede: By early 1998 banner ads paid the bills for much of the web, but placing them was crude. DoubleClick ran the servers that delivered ads to thousands of sites, and it used data about each visit to decide which ad to show. That let advertisers target people by interest, location, or time of day. The New York company went public in February 1998 as the leading name in online advertising.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Kevin O'Connor and Dwight Merriman founded DoubleClick in 1996. The bet was that technology could make web advertising measurable in a way print and television never were. DoubleClick sold ads across a network of sites and also licensed its ad-serving tools to large publishers. Its system counted every impression and click. That data made online advertising measurable in a new way.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: DoubleClick priced its offering at $17 a share in February 1998, and the stock rose dramatically through 1999. Its plan to merge web data with offline customer records led to a privacy uproar in 2000. Hellman & Friedman took the company private in 2005, and Google acquired DoubleClick in 2008 for about $3.1 billion, folding it into its advertising business. DoubleClick's ad tools became a core part of Google's advertising business.

cover.artwork: The Twin Brothers Ludwig and Emil Schulthess

dek: VeriSign issued digital certificates that proved websites were who they said they were, making secure online shopping possible.
lede: In 1998 shoppers were nervous about typing a credit card number into a website. Encryption could protect the data in transit, but people also needed proof that the site was genuine. VeriSign provided that proof. It issued digital certificates that browsers checked automatically, the basis for the padlock icon in the address bar. When VeriSign went public in January 1998, it was becoming a trusted third party for the whole web.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: VeriSign was spun out of RSA Data Security in 1995, with Jim Bidzos, RSA's leader, as its founding force. The bet was that online trust would need a neutral authority, much like a notary. VeriSign checked the identity of businesses and signed their certificates, and browsers came preloaded to trust VeriSign's signature. That trust made VeriSign central to online commerce.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: VeriSign priced its offering at $14 a share in January 1998, and the stock rose hugely in the boom. In 2000 it bought Network Solutions, which ran the registry for .com and .net domain names. VeriSign later sold its certificate business to Symantec and kept the registry. It remains a public company today. Its registry still handles every .com address on the internet.

cover.theme: a woman sealing a letter (trust and identity)

dek: Concord Communications sold software that measured and reported on the health and performance of corporate networks.
lede: In 1997 corporate networks were growing large and complex, and the people who ran them had little insight into how well they worked. Concord sold software called Network Health. It gathered data from routers, switches, and servers and turned it into clear reports on traffic, errors, and capacity. Managers could see trouble coming and plan upgrades. The Massachusetts company went public in October 1997.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was that networks had become critical to business, and that managers would pay for clear measures of their health. Concord's software worked with equipment from many vendors and produced reports that non-specialists could read. It sold to large companies and to service providers who needed to prove they met their promises to customers. It sold licenses and support, and its customers renewed year after year.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Concord priced its offering at $14 a share in October 1997. It grew through the internet boom and bought Empire Technologies and Aprisma to widen its products. Computer Associates acquired Concord in 2005, and its tools became part of CA's network management line. The offering gave it the funds to grow during the boom years. Concord was one of the steadier companies in this list, a software maker that sold to network managers and kept its focus on a single problem it understood well.

cover.artwork: View of the Battle Ground at Concord, Massachusetts

dek: Logility sold supply chain planning software that helped manufacturers and distributors forecast demand and move inventory.
lede: In the 1990s manufacturers and retailers were learning that much of their cost hid in the supply chain. Too much stock tied up cash, and too little lost sales. Logility, a unit of the Atlanta company American Software, sold planning software to address both. It forecast demand, planned inventory, and coordinated transport across a company's suppliers and warehouses. American Software spun out part of Logility in an offering in October 1997 and kept majority control.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The bet was that supply chain planning was a large market of its own, separate from general business software. Logility sold to consumer goods makers, distributors, and retailers. Its tools let planners look ahead, test scenarios, and share forecasts with partners, which cut waste and improved service. That focus suited companies that moved large volumes of goods through complex networks.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Logility priced its offering at $14.50 a share in October 1997. It stayed a small public company, with American Software as its controlling owner. In 2009 American Software bought the shares it did not already own and took Logility back in-house. The brand lived on as the company's supply chain business. The software it built continued to serve supply chain planners for years after.

dek: 8x8 began as a maker of video compression chips and became a provider of internet phone and video communications.
lede: In 1997 video over phone lines was a dream that kept almost arriving. 8x8, a Silicon Valley chip company, designed processors that compressed video and audio so they could travel over ordinary connections. Its chips went into videophones and conferencing systems. When it went public in July 1997, 8x8 was a small semiconductor company betting that people would want to see each other when they called.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Joe Parkinson and Chi-Ping Hsu founded the company in 1987. The bet was that compression was the key to sending rich media through narrow pipes. 8x8 designed chips and complete systems for video calling. As the internet grew, the company saw that voice and video calls could run over data networks, not just phone lines. The company would change its business more than once.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: 8x8 priced its offering at $6.50 a share in July 1997. The stock rose in the boom and fell in the crash, when the company was close to running out of money. 8x8 reinvented itself as a service provider, selling internet phone service to small businesses. It grew into a cloud communications company and remains publicly traded today. Few companies of its era changed course so completely.

dek: Amazon began as an online bookstore that offered more titles than any physical shop could hold.
lede: In May 1997 Amazon was a bookstore with no stores. It sold books through a website, shipped them from a warehouse in Seattle, and claimed a catalog of more than a million titles. Few people bought anything online yet, and many doubted they ever would. Amazon was losing money and planned to keep losing it to grow. Its offering that spring was modest by later standards, and the company called itself Earth's Biggest Bookstore.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Jeff Bezos left a hedge fund job in New York in 1994 and drove west to start the company. He chose books because there were millions of titles, too many for any shop to stock. The bet was that the web's unlimited shelf would beat physical stores on selection, and that customers would reward low prices and convenience. Bezos told investors to expect a long wait for profits.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Amazon priced its offering at $18 a share in May 1997. It added music, video, and then almost everything else, opened its site to other sellers, and survived the dot-com crash. It launched Prime, the Kindle, and Amazon Web Services, which turned its own computing systems into a business. Amazon remains a public company and one of the largest in the world.

dek: Go2Net ran MetaCrawler, a search engine that queried many other search engines at once, plus a network of web sites.
lede: In 1997 the web had many search engines, and each one covered only part of it. A search on one engine could miss pages that another found. Go2Net's MetaCrawler sent a single query to several engines at once, then combined the results. The Seattle company added other sites and services around it. Go2Net went public in April 1997, early in the internet boom, with a small offering.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Russell Horowitz founded Go2Net in 1996. The bet was that the web needed a layer on top of existing tools, one that saved people time by gathering results into one page. Go2Net licensed MetaCrawler from the University of Washington, where it began as a research project. It earned money from advertising on its growing network of sites. Go2Net also ran other web properties built around games and finance.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Go2Net priced its offering at $8 a share in April 1997. The stock rose many times over during the boom, helped by an investment from Paul Allen's Vulcan Ventures. In 2000 Go2Net merged with InfoSpace in a stock deal worth about $4 billion at announcement. MetaCrawler and Dogpile, which Go2Net had acquired, lived on under InfoSpace. It was one of the final big deals of the boom.

cover.theme: a fisherman mending a net (the net)

dek: CNET produced technology news and reviews on television and the web, guiding a generation of new computer buyers.
lede: In 1996 the computer industry was booming, and millions of people were buying their first PC or going online for the first time. CNET set out to explain it all. It produced television shows about technology on cable channels and built a group of websites with news, reviews, and software downloads. The San Francisco company went public in July 1996, one of the first media companies built for the internet age.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Halsey Minor founded CNET in 1992, and Shelby Bonnie joined him early and later ran the company. The bet was that technology was becoming a mainstream subject, worthy of its own network. CNET used television to build its brand and the web to reach readers directly. Its sites, including Download.com and News.com, became essential stops for computer users. It also sold advertising to the technology companies its readers followed.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: CNET priced its offering at $16 a share in July 1996. It grew through the boom, bought comparison shopping site mySimon and the media company ZDNet, and survived the crash as one of the largest web publishers. CBS acquired CNET in 2008 for about $1.8 billion. The brand later passed to Red Ventures and continues today. Its reviews still guide shoppers.

dek: A.D.A.M. made interactive anatomy software and later health information content for consumers and medical education.
lede: In 1995 the CD-ROM was the new medium of learning, and A.D.A.M. used it to open the human body. Its software let students peel back layers of anatomy, from skin to bone, on a personal computer. The name stood for Animated Dissection of Anatomy for Medicine. The Atlanta company sold to schools, medical students, and families, and it went public in November 1995, just as the web began to draw attention away from CD-ROMs.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: A.D.A.M. was founded in Atlanta in 1990. The bet was that detailed medical illustration, delivered by computer, could teach anatomy better than textbooks. The company built a large library of accurate images and animations. It sold versions for medical schools and simpler ones for home and school use. The images became its main asset, and the company would reuse them for decades in new formats.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: A.D.A.M. priced its offering at $12 a share in November 1995. As CD-ROMs faded, the company turned its library into online health content, which it licensed to hospitals, health sites, and insurers. It later added benefits technology for employers. Ebix, the Atlanta insurance software company, acquired A.D.A.M. in 2011 for about $66 million. Its anatomy library outlived the medium it was built for.
